data.title: Old Krištof – a legend from the Kamenec hillfort
data.excerpt: The second legend tied to the Kamenec hillfort below Vtáčnik tells of the widowed Krištof, whipped in the lord's forest in 1650, and of the gold ducats he dug out of a fiery rock. We publish it with the kind permission of its author, Iveta Géczyová, director of the Upper Nitra Museum in Prievidza.
data.metaTitle: Old Krištof – a legend from the Kamenec hillfort
data.metaDescription: The second legend tied to the Kamenec hillfort below Vtáčnik, together with the current threat to the Hrádok site from planned andesite quarrying.

timeline.title: Krištof goes into the lord's forest
timeline.description: On a spring day in 1650 the widowed Krištof, left with seven children, went into the forest of the lord of the castle to gather wood; he was caught and punished with a whip.

timeline.title: A mysterious voice and the treasure in the rock
timeline.description: The injured Krištof heard a mysterious voice that led him to a fiery rock; after digging through the boulder with his pickaxe he found gold ducats, with which he provided for his children.

timeline.title: Krištof's apparition
timeline.description: According to the legend, Krištof's figure with a pickaxe still appears to this day whenever great fires break out in the hills above the village.

children.text: With the kind permission of the author, PhDr. Iveta Géczyová, director of the Upper Nitra Museum in Prievidza, we bring you the second legend connected with the Kamenec hillfort below Vtáčnik / Bystričany.

In this connection I would draw attention to an issue that troubles more than one person interested in the history, hiking or rock climbing around Hrádok. A quarrying company intends to extract andesite there, and there is a danger that the extraction will damage the Hrádok site itself.

There is mystery in the hills above Bystričany. The old trees rustling in the wind and the dark black rocks peering out at the bends of the paths conceal riddles, and with them the long-forgotten life of the owners of the castle, built on a high crag so that its beauty could be seen far and wide. The castle's high walls and its tower rose into the sky, displaying the power and the wealth of its ruler. Everything belonged to him: the forests, the meadows, the fields, and even those people who grew a scrap of sustenance on their little plots for their children, but above all for him, the unkind and greedy lord. More than once they begged for a crust of bread, a little gruel or grain, but his heart remained as unyielding as the rock on which his castle stood.

On one of the spring days of the year of Our Lord 1650, when winter had not yet wholly left the land and the summit of Vtáčnik was still white with snow, Krištof too set out into the forest to look for a few pieces of wood. His wife had died only that winter, and seven children were left at home with him. He had to provide for them: to heat the log cottage, to get food and to look after the cow. The winter had been harsh, all the wood he had prepared that autumn was already spent, and a merciless cold poured from every corner of the house. He knew well that he was going into a forest belonging to the lord of the castle. Yet he believed he would manage to soften the lord's heart, should he be found gathering wood. It was still early morning, and so he hurried. He set off higher up, where no one was to discover him. He did not even take an axe, only a small pickaxe, reckoning that it would serve him well enough. He would lever up the root of a leaning, withering tree and drag it home. He crouched down — quickly, quickly to get the wood, and then he would run down through the dense thicket to the village, slip through the first gap between the houses, and he would already be in his own log cottage. No one would see him. He had not yet laid hold of the first dry branch when he heard the neighing of a horse in the distance. And then hoofbeats, stronger and stronger, as though Lucifer himself were coming with all his crew… It was the lord of the castle, who with his whole boisterous entourage stood beside him on his steed. He asked him mockingly: “And do you know that you are taking what is mine, you wretch?” “Oh, my lord, forgive me,” he began to plead imploringly. “This winter my wife Anka died and the children, my poor little ones, have nothing to eat. The cold is harsh, so at least a little of this dry wood for the stove…” he went on with his entreaty. But the lord of the castle did not let him finish: “So you have taken a fancy to warmth — but from what is mine, never indeed. No one will ever have what belongs to me alone. Do you understand? Be off with you!” And he was already raising his hand with the whip. He lashed once, twice, three times, but by then Krištof felt nothing at all. Tears flooded his face, and his heart went numb. Why is there so much malice and iniquity? One man has much, another little and a third nothing at all, ran through his mind. He still heard the lord conferring with the others about what to do with him. Then someone from the lordly company suggested that this good-for-nothing, this wretched thief, should simply be left there, for the beasts were only waiting for it. But Krištof no longer took this in, because the thought of his children was stronger. His own fate did not concern him, and he thought only and only of his children, of what would become of them and how they would live without him.

He had no idea how many hours he had lain in the forest beside the fallen dry tree when suddenly he felt a pleasant breeze, as though a warm human hand were stroking him. The breeze grew stronger, and Krištof did not know whether he was merely dreaming it all. He got to his feet, and then he fully realised what had happened. The pickaxe still clenched in his hand and the ground trampled all around were the proof that it had all been real. But the rest was strange: the gently blowing wind and a voice sounding from afar, calling his name: “Krištóóóf, Krištóóóf, come along after me.” He did not know what to do. Some mysterious force drew him towards a mighty rock that he had never seen before and had never even heard of. Well then, into the Lord God's hands, he thought, and let himself be led by the voice and the warm breeze. As he came closer to the rock he saw a light, tiny but bright and flickering, and an ever brighter glow blinded his eyes. Timidly and incredulously he nevertheless walked on, his mind on his children. And suddenly fiery flames burst from the rock; he took fright and stepped back. But the mysterious voice commanded firmly: “Krištof, think of the children and of their lives! Do not be afraid, and do what must be done!” The thought of the children roused him again, and so he gave himself over to the voice and its instructions. First he stepped across the bands of fire and found himself before a great boulder. The voice bade him grip the pickaxe firmly and dig. He struck once, a second and a third time, and the rock did not budge. He stopped counting and dug on in silence. He lost all sense of time and simply dug. As he straightened his back, wiping the sweat from his brow, he noticed a small opening, just large enough for a hand to be pushed through. And so he reached into the open hole with his hand. He felt something hard and round, took a handful of the small things and drew his hand out. He stared in disbelief at gold ducats. He had never seen so much gold, and so he thrust his hand under the stone again and took out another handful, and yet another. When he had a fine little heap of them, the mysterious voice spoke again. “Krištof, leave some for the others too… there are still plenty of poor people.” Krištof tied the little heap of money into a bundle, took up the pickaxe and set off for the village. He did not see the fiery tongues of flame flare up again, he did not hear the roar, he took in nothing. He was with his children once more, thinking about what he would do with the mysterious treasure.

From that day on things began to go better for Krištof's family. From the mysterious treasure — which, as he told himself, was recompense for the outrages of the powerful lord — he bought fields and began to farm. He never went back to that place and never revealed to anyone what had happened in the forest above the village. People merely shook their heads in bewilderment at where he had got so much property.

And only after many years, whenever a great fire broke out in the village, a mysterious figure with a pickaxe could be seen walking out of the village. Without doubt it was Krištof. He had gone out into the forest again for wood and for the treasure hidden in the mighty rocks below Vtáčnik.
